title: Docker Security Notes: Locking Down Containers
summary: Dense handwritten study notes covering how to harden Docker containers: non-root users, Linux capabilities, seccomp, read-only filesystems, image scanning, and secret handling.

chapters.title: 1. Threat Model: What Can Go Wrong
points: Containers are processes isolated by kernel namespaces (pid, net, mnt, user) and cgroups — not VMs; they share the host kernel
Kernel exploits matter most: a container breakout is usually a kernel vuln or misused privileged syscall path
Attack surfaces: container engine (dockerd), host kernel, mounted host paths, container network, and the image itself
Default Docker is NOT a security boundary: root in container ≈ root on host for kernel-level access unless user namespaces are used
Threat actors: malicious image content (supply chain), compromised app inside a container (runtime escape), leaked secrets
Defense in depth layers: non-root user → drop capabilities → seccomp filters → read-only FS → scanned images → managed secrets
Rule of thumb: each layer reduces blast radius; no single control stops every escape vector
Privileged mode (--privileged) removes nearly all isolation — treat as a red flag in any Dockerfile or run command

chapters.title: 2. Running as Non-Root
points: Why: processes running as UID 0 in-container inherit kernel-level power; many historic escapes required root
Dockerfile: USER appuser after installing packages; create with RUN adduser --system --no-create-home appuser (or groupadd/useradd)
Runtime override: docker run --user 1000:1000 works even for images that default to root
Kubernetes parallel: runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser in securityContext; Pod admission can enforce it
Gotcha: files created as root before USER stay root-owned — chmod/chown them first or bind mounts fail on write
Ports < 1024 are privileged: use high ports (8080) or set NET_BIND_SERVICE capability / sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start
User namespaces (userns-remap) map container root → unprivileged host UID range; adds isolation but breaks shared volumes and some images
HOME env: set ENV HOME=/home/appuser so tools writing dotfiles don't crash
Verify: docker exec <c> id → expect uid=1000(...), and docker inspect for the User field

chapters.title: 3. Linux Capabilities: Granular Root Powers
points: Root power is split into ~40 capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, ...); Docker grants a default subset
Default Docker drop list removes dangerous ones: CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mount, namespaces), CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, CAP_MKNOD
docker run --cap-drop=ALL then --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE: whitelist only what the app needs
CAP_SYS_ADMIN is 'the new root' — granting it approximates full root; avoid unless a container legitimately manages mounts/namespaces
Inspect a running container's caps: docker exec <c> sh -c 'cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap' then decode with capsh --decode
capsh --print inside the container shows effective, permitted, bounding sets — great for auditing
File capabilities (setcap) can grant a single binary a cap without container-wide privileges, e.g. setcap cap_net_bind_service+ep on nginx
Gotcha: --cap-add can't restore caps already dropped from the bounding set; restart with correct flags
Rule: --privileged = all caps + devices + cgroup write — never in production

chapters.title: 4. Seccomp: Syscall Firewalls
points: Seccomp (secure computing mode) filters which syscalls a process may call, via BPF rules attached at process start
Docker's default seccomp profile blocks ~44 risky syscalls (kexec_load, open_by_handle_at, keyctl...) and permits the rest
Profiles are JSON: list defaultAction (e.g. SCMP_ACT_ERRNO) plus allowed syscalls with args-based conditions
Custom profile: docker run --security-opt seccomp=/path/profile.json; --security-opt seccomp=unconfined disables entirely
Recent kernels: seccomp can use notify action to proxy syscalls to a supervisor (used by gVisor-style designs)
Seccomp ≠ capabilities: caps gate what resources you may touch; seccomp gates which kernel entry points exist
Debugging: EPERM on weird ops often means seccomp; use strace outside the filter to find the blocked syscall
Gotcha: seccomp is not namespaced — profile applies per container, set at run time, not in the image
Keep profiles minimal: allowlist only syscalls your runtime needs; use tools like `must`-mode tracing (strace -c) to derive the set

chapters.title: 5. Read-Only Filesystems & Resource Limits
points: docker run --read-only mounts the container's root filesystem read-only — tamper-proofing and ransomware resistance
Writable space: --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m for temp dirs; --mount type=tmpfs for selective writes
Volumes remain writable under a read-only rootfs; give the app only the volume paths it needs
Apps that write in-place (PID files, caches, logs) break on read-only roots — fix paths via env config or tmpfs
noexec on tmpfs prevents executing downloaded payloads; nosuid ignores setuid bits in writable areas
Pair read-only with --cap-drop=ALL: even a compromised process has no writable code path and no root powers
cgroup limits contain damage: --memory, --pids-limit (stops fork bombs), --cpus — an escaped process still hits limits
Don't disable the OOM-adjacent safety: memory limits force attackers into resource-constrained escapes
Gotcha: some base images (alpine apk, apt) need writable /var — do installs at build time, not runtime

chapters.title: 6. Image Hardening: Minimal Base Images
points: Every package in an image is attack surface and CVE load — prefer distroless, alpine, or scratch bases
Multi-stage builds: compile in a full toolchain image, COPY only the binary into a minimal runtime stage
Never ship build tools, package managers, or shells in runtime images — fewer tools = fewer post-exploit options
Pin base image digests: FROM node:20@sha256:<digest> for reproducible, tamper-checked builds
Run as non-root inside the Dockerfile (USER), COPY --chown instead of post-hoc chown layers
Use .dockerignore to keep secrets (.env, .git, keys) out of the build context — COPY . can leak them into layers
Multi-arch + reproducible builds reduce 'surprise' image drift; enable BuildKit for cleaner layer control
Don't store secrets in ENV or RUN lines — layer history preserves them forever (see chapter 10)
Static binaries (Go/Rust) make scratch images viable: ~10MB, zero package CVEs

chapters.title: 7. Image Scanning & Supply Chain
points: Scanners match installed packages against CVE databases: Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout, Snyk
Trivy usage: trivy image myapp:1.2 — reports OS packages, language deps (pip/npm), and config issues
Scan in CI on every build; fail the pipeline above a severity threshold: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
Prioritize by exploitability: a CRITICAL in a base-image lib you never execute can often be accepted; one in your runtime web server cannot
Rebuild base images regularly — most CVE fixes arrive by re-pulling an updated base, not editing your code
SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): trivy image --format cyclonedx generates an inventory; use it for audit and diffing
Content trust / signatures: docker content trust (Notary) or cosign verify ensures the image you run is the one that was built
Gotcha: scanning at build time only is a snapshot — rescan running/registried images on a schedule (new CVEs appear daily)
Pin versions in requirements.txt/package-lock so scans are deterministic and diffs meaningful

chapters.title: 8. Docker Socket, Daemon & Network isolation
points: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container = root on host: the socket API can spawn privileged containers
Safer alternatives to socket mounts: docker-socket-proxy restricting API verbs, or rootless Docker/Podman
Rootless Docker runs dockerd itself as unprivileged user with user namespaces — daemon compromise ≠ host root
Default bridge network is flat: all containers can reach each other — create user-defined networks and isolate per trust zone
--network=none for jobs that need no network; internal networks (internal: true) block external egress
Inter-container TLS/mTLS still matters inside the bridge — network proximity is not trust
Expose dockerd over TCP only with TLS and only if unavoidable; unauthenticated 2375 is instant host compromise
Gotcha: --link is legacy; use user-defined networks with DNS service names instead
Audit: docker network inspect and docker port to find accidental host-published ports (0.0.0.0 bindings)

chapters.title: 9. Runtime Detection & Hardened Runtimes
points: Controls reduce attack surface; runtime detectors catch what slips through: Falco, Sysdig, eBPF-based monitors
Falco rules flag suspicious behavior: shell spawned in nginx container, unexpected writes to /etc, outbound to odd IPs
gVisor: user-space kernel intercepting syscalls — huge seccomp-like reduction, at cost of per-syscall overhead
Kata Containers: lightweight VMs per container — kernel isolation like VMs, higher memory/startup cost
Trade-off spectrum: runc (fast, kernel-shared) → gVisor (syscall filtering) → Kata (VM boundary); pick by threat model and latency budget
AppArmor/SELinux add mandatory access control per container: --security-opt apparmor=profile (Docker's default profile exists)
Performance note: seccomp overhead is near-zero; gVisor adds meaningful syscall latency for I/O-heavy apps
Detect drift: compare running process list/image digest against expected (docker ps + image ID checks)
Post-incident: container filesystems are ephemeral — export evidence (docker cp) before the container dies

chapters.title: 10. Secrets Handling & Summary Checklist
points: Never bake secrets into images: ENV, ARG, and RUN layers persist in history (docker history shows every layer)
Build-time secrets: BuildKit mounts — RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmNPM_TOKEN npm install; secret never lands in a layer
Runtime secrets: Docker Swarm secrets (tmpfs-backed at /run/secrets/<name>) or Kubernetes Secrets + encryption at rest
K8s Secrets are base64, not encrypted by default — enable etcd encryption and RBAC on the secrets API
Inject via mounted files over environment variables: env vars leak via /proc/<pid>/environ, crash dumps, and child processes
External managers: Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SOPS for encrypted secrets in git; short-lived tokens beat static keys
Rotate after any exposure — deleting an image does not unpull it from mirrors, caches, or attacker machines
Gitleaks/trufflehog on the repo to stop .env and credentials entering the build context in the first place

Summary checklist: non-root USER → --cap-drop=ALL + needed caps → default/custom seccomp → --read-only + tmpfs → distroless pinned image → scanned CI → no socket mounts → secrets via BuildKit/swarm → runtime detection → resource limits
Security is layered trade-offs: each control costs a little convenience; apply all ten and a single failure rarely becomes a host compromise
